1. The animation shows how inflation affects a fixed income, using two illustrative retirees, Edna and Carl, and US consumer prices (CPI-U). Edna's income starts in January 1949. Carl's starts in January 1966. Each retiree has ten "crates" that stand for what their income buys. The label says "kept up: the last start month that did." The animation is labeled illustrative, US only, and "history, not a forecast."

2. In frames 1–3, Edna's row of ten crates is checked against prices at "+2% a year," and at year 20 all ten crates are still "lit." In frames 4–6, the view moves to a timeline. Edna's 20-year span (1949 to about 1969) is compared with Carl's span (1966 to 1986), and the two overlap in 1966–1969. Both rows of crates are shown at year 20, and Edna's are still all lit.

3. The overlap in 1966–1969 shows that both retirees lived through the same years of prices. Edna lived through them at the end of her 20 years. Carl lived through them at the start of his. The caption "same years of prices: her last, his first" says this. The implication is that whether a fixed payout keeps up with prices depends on which years you retire into. Edna's start month is the last one in the animation's history that kept up. Carl's span began in 1966, so by implication it did not. Frame 6 only shows Edna's crates as "all 10 still lit," and Carl's row is unlabeled. I'm inferring his outcome from the "last start month that did" caption.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that a fixed payout's buying power depends on the inflation of the decades after retirement, which no one can know in advance. They might also take away that past results from one start date don't guarantee the same result for another.

5. The takeaway in 4 is my own conclusion. The animation only presents the comparison and the "history, not a forecast" caveat. It doesn't tell the viewer to choose or avoid any payout option, and it doesn't mention the two options in the quote.
